claims.text: Molecular dynamics simulations can capture the size-dependent thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have lower melting points than larger particles.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are well equilibrated at room temperature.
The simulated intervention consists of thermal annealing by progressively increasing temperature.
Nanoparticles of several different sizes are simulated.
The simulations are conducted in vacuum or an inert atmosphere.
Nanoparticle size determines the surface-to-volume ratio.
Finite-size effects increase the relative contribution of surface energy in smaller nanoparticles.
The greater surface-energy contribution promotes melting at lower temperatures in smaller nanoparticles.
The simulations observed a systematic decrease in melting temperature with decreasing nanoparticle size.
The predicted size dependence agrees with classical surface-energy-based melting-point-depression theories.
Bulk or sufficiently large HEA simulations show higher thermal stability than smaller nanoparticles.
Synthesis-induced nonequilibrium states, oxidation, or environmental interactions may dominate the thermal response and invalidate the proposed size dependence.
The quantitative relationship between nanoparticle size and melting temperature in FeCuCrCoNi is uncertain.
A rapid increase in atomic displacement or changes in the radial distribution function can be used to identify melting.
Failure to observe a systematic melting-temperature decrease with decreasing particle size would falsify the hypothesis.
Qualitative disagreement between simulated and experimental melting behavior would falsify the hypothesis.
